title: Anas ibn Malik
hook: served the Prophet ten years and never once heard him ask, why did you do that

segments.voice: Yesterday, Abu Hurayrah, named for the little cat he carried. Your line was: father of the kitten. Did some creature get water or a gentler step from you? Day eight hundred thirty-eight.

A boy is sent on an errand. He says out loud that he won't go, though inside he means to. He heads out, and on the way through the market he comes upon some children playing, and there he stops. The errand waits. Then a hand takes him gently by the back of the neck. He looks up, and the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, is laughing. Little Anas, he says, did you go where I asked you? And the boy says, yes, I'm going now. That scene is in Sahih Muslim, told by the boy himself. Today: the servant who was never scolded.
screen: `AN ERRAND, AND A GAME.` → `A HAND ON THE NECK.` → `HE WAS LAUGHING.`

segments.voice: Anas ibn Malik came into the Prophet's household as a boy. Bukhari records his mother, Umm Sulaym, saying to the Prophet: Anas is your servant; pray for him. And the Prophet did. So Anas grew up in that house, running errands, watching, listening. Years later he summed up what he had seen in one sentence that both Bukhari and Muslim keep. I served the Prophet for ten years, Anas said, and he never said to me so much as uff. He never said, about something I had done, why did you do that? And never, about something I had left undone, why didn't you do that? Hold that up against an ordinary week. A boy in a busy household, and ten years of jobs. Some were done badly. Some were forgotten. Some, like the errand in the market, were put off while he stopped among children at play. Anas doesn't say he was perfect. He says he was never made to answer for it with a sharp word. And notice the word he picks: uff. Not a lecture. Not a punishment. The smallest sigh of annoyance, the noise people make before they even think. The Qur'an uses that same little word in the surah called the Night Journey, telling believers not to say uff to aging parents. Anas reports that he never heard even that much. Some teachers cite this hadith when they talk about the Prophet's character, and about how to treat anyone who works for you or under you: children, students, staff. Ten years of small failures, met with patience. That is the record a servant kept of his master.
screen: `YOUR SERVANT. PRAY FOR HIM.` · `TEN YEARS IN THE HOUSE.` · `NOT EVEN UFF.` · `NEVER: WHY DID YOU DO THAT?` · then, large: `TEN YEARS, NO SCOLDING.`

segments.voice: The practice: go a day without scolding. Settle, and breathe. Think of the person you are most likely to snap at today. A child, a coworker, someone at the counter, someone at home. See the small thing they might get wrong. The late reply, the dish left out, the job half done. Breathe in, and notice whether an uff starts to rise. Breathe out, and let it go before it reaches your mouth. Choose now what you'll say instead: a question, a joke, or nothing at all. If you pray, you can ask for patience with that one person. The bell holds the time.
Anas ibn Malik. Brought to the Prophet as a boy by his mother, he served in that house for ten years and said he never heard even a sigh of blame. Today's word.
Your line: ten years, no scolding. Today, when someone gets a small thing wrong, catch the uff before it leaves you, and ask instead of blame. Day eight hundred thirty-eight.

howItsDone: Muslims often cite Anas's report of ten years without a harsh word when teaching about the Prophet's character and about kindness to children, students and anyone who works for them.

pairs: brought her son and asked for a prayer

myth: Anas said he never made mistakes in the Prophet's house
he says the opposite: things done and left undone, and never a 'why did you do that?'
the Prophet found Anas among children in the market instead of on his errand, and laughed
Anas tells it in Sahih Muslim: a hand on the back of his neck, and laughter.
Anas came to the Prophet as a grown man
his mother Umm Sulaym offered him as the Prophet's servant and asked for a prayer, and Muslim's report finds him among children in the market.

fork.setup: you're the Prophet. the boy you sent on an errand has stopped among children playing in the market. what do you do?
options: scold him in front of the other children.
take him by the neck, laughing, and ask if he went.
send someone else and say nothing.
fork.reveal: Anas says he looked up and the Prophet was laughing: did you go where I asked? yes, I'm going.

original.note: Arabic: the smallest sound of annoyance, the word Anas says he never heard.

trapdoor: what you thought: a servant boy who did everything right.
what it means: a boy who forgot things and dawdled, and was never met with even a sigh of blame.
what a scholar hears: uff, the same tiny word the Qur'an tells believers not to say to aging parents (17:23).

sources.ref: Sahih Muslim 2309 / Sahih al-Bukhari 6038 (ten years, never uff, never why did you do that)
Sahih Muslim 2310 (the errand, the children playing, 'Unays, did you go?')
Sahih al-Bukhari 6334 (Umm Sulaym: Anas is your little servant, pray for him)

notes: Hadith numbers cited from memory (Muslim 2309, 2310; Bukhari 6038, 6334); confirm.
Muslim 2310 uses the diminutive 'Unays'; rendered as 'little Anas'. Confirm.
Myth item: some versions of 6038 mention the period as nine or ten years; the cited Muslim/Bukhari wording says ten. Confirm.
'Teachers cite this hadith when they talk about...' is a general description of how the hadith is used; confirm.

Editor: Muslim 2310 says Anas came upon children playing, not that he joined them, so hook, teach, myth and fork now say he stopped among them; 'your little servant' changed to 'your servant' to match Bukhari 6334; 'teachers cite' softened to 'some teachers'; practice no longer tells the listener an uff is rising.
Audit (fresh read): checked against the cited reports; no change needed.
